title: Chapter 181 – The Alpha's Heart
html:
[The Founders' Shaft – Lin Jian]

Bell's rule is simple, and she repeats it three times in the infirmary before she will let him stand: he is not to go anywhere he cannot be carried out of.

"The Shaft is two miles of dark," she says. She is sitting on the edge of his cot with a bowl of black paste in her lap and her sleeves pushed to the elbow, and she is not looking at his face. She is looking at his hands. "You are going into the lair of the thing that killed Lan Wen."

"The thing did not kill Lan Wen. The nail killed Lan Wen."

"Don't be clever. I haven't the temper for it." Bell scoops a thick smear of the paste and presses it, with some violence, into the hollow of his wrist. It stings. It smells of cloves and wet iron. "This is the last of the lung salve. After this I have the pills, and the pills do not work on the part that is really dying. You understand that."

"I understand."

"You say that every time." Her voice cracks, and she stops. She is thirty-seven, a spare, short-haired, hard-handed woman with ink under her nails and a scar across her lip. She has the best hands in the Garden. She has been using them for six days to patch the gaps in a tide of broken bodies, and she has not once complained. "I am so tired of being the one who says rest, Jian. I am so tired of it. You never do."

He takes her hand. It is warm and rough and shaking.

"I am going to do one more thing," he says. "Then I am going to rest. I will rest for as long as I have left. I will sit in the kitchen and listen to Qinghe shout at the pot. I will let you give me every bitter tea you can brew." He holds her eyes. "But Lan Wen asked me to find the nail, and a thousand sleepers in the Hall are waiting on whatever's at the end of it. I cannot be the man who let that wait."

Bell is silent a long moment.

"You'll take Feng," she says.

"Feng?"

"He can hear seams. He heard the cellar door at the Dock before the guard had finished knocking. He can find the way through that dark better than any lamp." She wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist. "And you'll take Dai. She's built like a bull. If you fall, she can carry you."

"Bell."

"Don't thank me." She stands and presses the bowl into his hands. "Drink the rest of the tea. Then go. And Jian."

"Yes?"

"Come back and let me be angry at you."

He promises. It is easy to promise. He has been promising things all week.

* * *

They go down at noon, by the Founders' Shaft, and the first thing he notices is that the beasts have left it clean.

The great tunnel runs south from the Dock, twenty feet wide and as high, cut by hands that knew their trade. The walls are smooth. The floor is dressed. Every ten paces, set into the stone, a socket of black iron waits for a torch that has not been lit in a thousand years. He has brought a lantern, and Feng carries another, and Dai walks behind with a spear and a coil of rope. Their three small lights make a trembling bubble in the dark.

And all along the tunnel, on both sides, the Gnashers lie asleep.

It is a strange sight. A river of dark gray hide, ten feet thick, packed shoulder to shoulder against the walls and breathing slowly, with their blunt heads laid on their forelegs like hounds before a fire. They do not stir as the three walk past. A few twitch. One snorts and rolls over. Dai's grip on her spear whitens, but Feng pats the nearest flank as he passes, the way one pats a cart-horse.

"They're tired," he whispers. He is bent over, stooped like a question mark, with his ear tilted. "The thread let go of them. They don't know where they are."

"Can you hear the way?"

"I hear everything, lad. That's the trouble." He cocks his head. "There's a seam ahead. A big one. It runs down and down. And at the end there's... oh." He stops.

"What?"

"A heartbeat. Slow. Slower than a mountain." Feng's wrinkled face goes soft with awe. "It's the biggest I ever heard. I think it's asleep."

Jian lifts his lantern.

The tunnel bends, and at the bend the floor drops away into a ramp, and the ramp winds down, spiralling, into a dark that his light cannot touch. A warm breath rises out of it. It smells of rain on hot stone, and of deep, deep earth, and under that of something he cannot name, a faint sweetness, like milk.

"Stay close," he says.

* * *

The chamber at the bottom is the size of a cathedral, and it is full of white roots.

They fill the whole space. They spring from the walls and the roof and the floor, a forest of pale fibers as thick as a man's thigh and fine as a hair, interlaced and knotted and twisted into columns, arches, whorls. They glow faintly from within, a soft silver-blue, so that the entire great cavern shines like the inside of a pearl. Water drips somewhere. The warmth is almost tropical.

And in the midst of it, rising from the floor like a hill, lies a body.

It is a Moonhorn. He knows the name from the Beast Mountains' old tales, but he has never seen one, nor has any living man. It is a beast the size of a barn: a vast white deer-shape, antlered, long-legged, heavy as a boulder, with a hide the color of old ivory and a single great spiral horn that rises from its brow and passes through the roof into the rock above. Its eyes are shut. Its sides rise and fall, once in a hundred of Jian's breaths. The roots grow out of its flanks, and its hide, and its mane, and run away into the walls. It is a part of the mountain. It has been here so long it has grown into the stone.

"Oh," says Dai, very softly. "Oh, gods."

"Don't touch it."

"I wasn't going to."

"Don't look at the horn." Jian lowers his lantern. "I think it is listening."

He walks forward. His boots make no sound on the soft white floor. He passes under an arch of roots and across a bridge of knotted fibers and stops at the foot of the great flank, so close he can feel the animal's heat on his face. The sweetness is stronger here. He thinks of a kitchen, of Qinghe, of rice-milk in a bowl.

He lays his hand on the hide.

Keeper, says the Moonhorn.

It is not a voice. It is a presence in the skull, vast and slow and gentle. He feels it uncurl in his mind like a great cat stretching, and he realizes with a start that it has been awake for some time, watching him, with the patient attention of a creature who has had a long while to learn how.

Keeper, it says. You came. I did not think anyone would.

"I am Lin Jian."

I know your name. I have heard it in the threads. A pause, like a great breath. I am sorry. I did not mean to hurt your captain. I did not mean to hurt any of them. I could not stop my hands.

"Lan Wen said as much."

She was very brave. She saw me. There is something infinitely sad in the voice. No one has seen me in a thousand years. I had forgotten what it was to be seen.

"Why can't you stop?"

Because of the nail.

* * *

It shows him, and the showing is a kind of seeing.

The chamber dims. The roots fade, and the white flank under his hand dissolves, and he finds himself standing in a vast, bright, empty place with the Moonhorn rearing before him like a mountain of living light. It is young. It is not what it is now. It stands tall on four slender legs, with its horn gleaming, and around its feet a whole herd of lesser beasts lies sleeping, hundreds, thousands, a hundred kinds, all the creatures of the Beast Mountains in a single warm huddle.

I was set to keep them, says the Moonhorn. The Founders asked me. They were kind. They said, there is a door below the mountain, and the door must stay shut, and the beasts must stay the guardians of it. They said I would be the Alpha, the oldest, the one who is listened to. A wistful note. I said yes. I thought it an honor.

The scene shifts. The young Moonhorn lies in a dark chamber with its head on its paws, and a figure bends over it. A woman. Tall, hooded, veiled, with a long silver rod in her hands. The rod ends in a thin glittering wire as fine as a thread.

She was one of the nine, says the Moonhorn. The Veiled. She said it was necessary. She said the door would be opened one day, from the other side, and the herd would wake and scatter, and the thing the Founders had sealed would escape. He said I must be bound, to hold the herd.

The wire goes in.

It goes in behind the great animal's breastbone, slow and precise, and the Moonhorn cries out. It is a cry the whole mountain remembers. The wire lights, blue and cold, and a fine silver thread runs out of it across the floor to the sleeping herd, and every beast in the chamber shudders and sits up.

It did not hurt, says the Moonhorn. Not the nail. What hurt was afterward. When I could hear them. All of them. In my head, at once, their hunger and their fear and their grief, a thousand years of it. I had been one voice. I became a choir.

"And the door?"

It was opened. From the other side. The vision darkens. Six days ago. By the child's bell. And the herd woke, and the nail tightened, and the one who holds the other end of the wire... pulled.

"Who holds the other end?"

I do not know. The enormous head turns. In the great dark eyes, Jian sees the whole sad sweep of a thousand years. But I have felt him, once or twice. A man in a glass room, very far away, with a wire under his skin. He is trying to stop. I think he does not know he is doing it.

Jian stands very still.

Ethan, he thinks.

* * *

The vision breaks. He is back in the chamber, with his hand on the hide, and Dai is gripping his sleeve, and Feng's lantern is shaking.

"You went white," says Dai. "You went white as paper. You were standing there ten minutes."

"I was shown something."

"Was it bad?"

"No." He draws a long breath. "It was sad."

Keeper, says the Moonhorn. Will you take it out?

He looks at the creature. He looks at the roots and the hide and the great slow rise and fall of its side. He looks, finally, at the spot behind its breastbone where a thin pale light burns through the ivory fur: a thread of cold blue, bright as a star, driven in to the hilt.

"Will it kill you?" he asks.

Yes.

"All at once?"

Almost. I will have a few breaths. The mind-voice is steady. I have been holding on for a thousand years, Keeper. I think I have earned the right to put it down.

"What happens to the herd?"

They wake. They remember what they are. Most will go home. A faint warmth. Some will not. Some have forgotten the way. You will have to be kind to them.

"I'll try."

And there is one thing more. The great head lowers. A fleck of light, no bigger than a grain of rice, glimmers at the base of the spiral horn. I carry a core. It is old. It is very large. When I die, it will go out unless something takes it. I would like it to be you.

"Me?"

You are failing, Keeper. I can feel it. The Core in your belly is a cinder. I have the oldest fire in the valley. The faintest smile. It would be a waste to bury it.

He opens his mouth to refuse. He does not.

"There will be a cost," he says.

Everything has a cost.

"I mean to you. To me." He swallows. "It will remember you. It will carry your grief."

Yes, says the Moonhorn. That is the only reason I am offering. It lowers its head till the huge ivory brow rests against the floor. Take the nail, Keeper. And then sit with me a while. I have not had company in so long.

* * *

The nail comes out in three movements.

He does it with both hands, kneeling in the white fur, with Feng holding the lantern and Dai at his shoulder murmuring something under her breath. It is warm, not cold. A thin silver wire, finer than any thread he has seen, sunk deep into the body of the beast, and when he takes hold of it, he feels a hum run up his arms into his teeth. A voice, small, distant, panicked, says no, no, I didn't mean to, and he knows whose it is.

It is all right, he thinks, to the other end of the wire. To a man in a glass room, a thousand miles away, who is a working copy of himself. It is all right, Ethan. Let go.

He pulls.

The wire slides out in a single bright line, like a thread drawn through silk. There is no blood. There is only light, a flood of it, rising from the wound in a column of silver-blue that fills the chamber to the roof. The roots flare. The walls sing. The Moonhorn rears its head, once, and gives a cry that is not pain at all.

It is a sound like an ending sigh, enormous and glad.

Thank you, it says.

Sit with me, it says. Only a moment.

He sits. He puts his back against the warm flank and his hand on the great slow rib, and the Moonhorn shows him the Beast Mountains, as they were. A morning in spring, with mist in the pines. A river running blue over white stones. A hundred young beasts rolling in the grass, a fawn with spotted flanks butting at his mother's legs, an owl the size of a house gliding low over a meadow of flowers. The old Alpha walks among them, young and tall, and the herd turns its heads to watch her pass. They are glad. They are not afraid. It is the happiest picture he has ever been shown.

That is what I kept, says the Moonhorn. Not a door. A morning.

"It is a good morning."

Yes. The voice is already far away. Tell them, when they ask, that I was not angry. I was only tired. And that I was looked after, at the end.

"I will tell them."

Good. Good. A last, vast, contented sigh. Now go and eat my fire, Keeper, and be well.

The light fades. The great head sinks. The sides, which have been rising and falling for a thousand years, rise one last time, and fall, and do not rise again.

For a long moment no one speaks. Even the roots have gone dark.

Then, in the stillness, a thin high keening begins, far off, up the tunnel, from the sleeping herd. It spreads. It becomes a wail. A thousand Gnashers lift their heads in the dark, and mourn.

* * *

They wait a long time, afterward, in the cold glow of the roots, and no one has the heart to leave.

The wailing in the tunnel rises and falls. It is not one voice but thousands, a vast low chorus of grief, passing from throat to throat down the long dark corridor. Dai stands with her spear at the rest and her head bowed. Feng sits cross-legged on the floor with his hands over his ears and tears running down his seamed cheeks, rocking.

"I can hear them," he says. "Every one. They're saying her name."

"What is her name?"

"They don't say a name. It's a shape. Like... a mother." He wipes his face. "I never knew animals could do that."

Footsteps, then, in the tunnel above: slow, heavy, shuffling. A shape appears at the head of the ramp, black against the faint light. It is a Gnasher, a young one, small for its kind, no larger than a pony. It stands at the top of the spiral and stares down at them with its small red eyes. Dai's spear comes up.

"Don't," says Jian.

The creature descends. It moves like a sleepwalker, stiff-legged, unsteady, and crosses the white floor to the Moonhorn's flank. There it stops. It sniffs the cold hide. It lowers its blunt head, and presses its forehead against the great still shoulder, and makes a low sound in its throat, a soft broken whine, like a dog that has lost its master.

Then it turns its head and looks at Jian.

There is no hunger in the eyes. There is only a bewildered, enormous sadness, and under it, dimly, a question.

"She's gone home," Jian says quietly. "You can go home, too."

The Gnasher considers this. Then, slowly, it backs away from the body, turns, and climbs the ramp into the dark. Behind it, in the tunnel, the wailing begins to change. It does not stop. But it thins, and lengthens, and grows less like a cry and more like a song.

"They're leaving," says Feng, listening. "All of them. Going south, through the old tunnels. They know the way."

"Good," says Jian.

He stays with the body a moment longer, with his hand on the cooling flank.

* * *

The core is the size of a plum.

It lies in the hollow at the base of the horn, in a nest of pale roots, and when he lifts it out it is warm, and heavy, and faintly shining, a deep, dense, milky-gold sphere with a spiral of silver at its heart. It is the most beautiful object he has ever held. It is also, quite plainly, a living thing. He feels it pulse against his palm, slow and patient, like a second heart.

"Do you know how to eat it?" says Dai, in a hushed voice.

"No."

"Then how will you...?"

"I think," says Jian slowly, "that it knows."

He sits down on the floor of the chamber, with his back against the great cold flank, and closes his eyes. He opens his tunic. He sets the core against the place beneath his breastbone, where his own cinder of a Core lies buried in the failing flesh. And he does the one thing that Kito taught him, at the end, without words: he stops pushing, and lets.

The core sinks in.

It is not painless. A heat spreads outward from his belly, up through his ribs and down through his thighs, so sudden and fierce that he cries out. The cinder in his abdomen flares. It drinks. He feels the gold in him sing, a thin high bell-note, and then a rush as of snow-water over dry riverbed, filling every crack. His lungs open. His heart stutters, and steadies, and beats once, hard.

His Core is whole.

It is not what it was. It is more. The old cinder has become a coal, and the coal a small bright sun, and around its edge, very faintly, a spiral of silver turns.

```
NOTICE
Foreign core integrated: Moonhorn (old).
Core integrity: 47% -> 88%
Core stage: Mid (provisional)
Keystone feed: restored (source: foreign core, 14-day charge)
Estimated remaining: 13 wks, 5 d (unchanged)
SCAN: UNLOCKED (conditional)
Condition: each scan consumes 1 day of lifespan.
Advice: USE SPARINGLY.
```

He reads it three times. He does not trust it.

The grief arrives a breath later.

He had been warned. He thought he understood. But a thousand years of loss cannot be understood; it can only be borne. It comes up through the new fire like a tide, the whole slow sorrow of the Alpha, every herd-mother she failed to save, every winter she lay awake listening to a thousand hungers she could not still. He feels the nail's absence as a phantom ache behind his own breastbone. He feels the long dull ache of a promise kept past its time.

He bows over his knees and weeps.

It is not his weeping. He knows that. It is hers, passing through him like wind through a keyhole. But it is real, and it is enormous, and for a long time he cannot stop. Feng's hand comes down on his shoulder. Dai crouches and says nothing. They wait, two old fools in a white cave, while a man they love learns what it is to carry another creature's heart.

When it passes, he is lighter. Not freed. Lighter. The grief is still there, folded small at the center of the Core, a patient quiet weight, like a stone in a pocket. He thinks he will carry it for the rest of his life.

It will not be a long life. He finds, a little to his surprise, that this makes it easier.

Scan unlocked.

He has not had Scan since the loop opened. He has lived four months without the one tool he trusted above all others, and in all that time he has been a man blind and groping, with a staff and a good heart and nothing else. It is a bright small shock to have it back. It feels like a hand laid on his shoulder.

A day, he thinks. Each time.

"Jian?" says Feng, anxiously. "Lad? Are you well?"

"I'm well." He opens his eyes. They are, he finds, quite clear. "Feng. Give me the nail."

The old man hands it over. It lies across his palm, a fine silver wire as long as his forearm, glimmering faintly. He looks at it for a long time.

Then, for the first time in months, he lifts his hand and says, in his mind, the one word he has not dared to say.

Scan.

The panel opens. It is brighter than he remembers.

```
SCAN: object
Type: Gate lead (monofilament, silver-lattice)
Origin: Chamber C-1 (Ethan Cole, working copy)
Function: remote command link, 1 of 8
Status: severed at beast end; live at source
Warning: 7 leads remain in the valley.
```

Seven, he thinks. Seven more beasts like her, somewhere in the valley, with a nail of their own.

He does the arithmetic without wanting to. One day, to learn what a thing is. Seven leads, seven beasts, seven wires. Perhaps a week of his life, in all, to find them and read them and decide what to do. It is not a great sum. It is also not a small one, from a man who has counted his days in dozens. He understands now what the panel meant by use sparingly. The cost is not the number. The cost is knowing that every time he looks, he is choosing what to look at.

He closes his hand. The wire is warm against his skin, and somewhere very far away, in a glass room, a man with his own face is crying.
